<pasted_content id="ba41">
I’m looking to build my personal brand. Part of that is finally building a site for myself. I was recently laid off (in July) and the job market has not been great. I have 18 years of experience but my presence on the web is pretty limited. I want to build out a site that acts sort of like a portfolio/resume but also a home for me to start writing blog posts that I’ll share on X, LinkedIn, etc. There are two files in this project right now (both Markdown files). The IDEATION.md file is sort of just a brain dump of ideas. My ADHD brain works this way. I need you to help not only refine these ideas, but also to fill in gaps where I’m likely missing opportunities whether it’s in content for the site or the design/build itself. 

The long term goal is for me to have a Design System in Figma that uses the modern Figma design tokens/variables that will then go to something like Style Dictionary (or another alternative) to Storybook to the live site. The purpose of this design/build is for it to basically be a portfolio piece in itself. The idea is to build my core brand but then demonstrate the Design System build by simply allowing site visitors to “remix” the site which would keep the markup the same but tokens would change making the site look like a different site/brand. Sort of a throw back to the old CSS Zen Garden days of the early 2000s. 

We will be using the impeccable style skills/plugin to make sure there is no “AI Slop” and that our end result looks fresh, modern, clean, and has a little Wow factor. Impeccable will help us with that: https://impeccable.style/llms.txt

The CONTENT.md file is not prescriptive. This is a document that I worked with Claude on before. So, the content itself is fine and we will likely use a lot of it, but I want you and I to have design freedom to accomplish our goals. So, treat the CONTENT.md file as just that, some content, but not the decisions on where things will live or where the content will appear on the site, etc. 

Before we even think about designing and building this, I’d like to plan out how we should approach this. Do you want to review the documents in the project so far and come up with some questions that you have to help build up your context and understanding of what we’re planning to do, then jump into actual planning before designing and building? 
</pasted_content id="ba41">

# Thoughts, notes, open questions for jarodtaylor.com

**Companion file:** `CONTENT.md`

---

## Problem

Jarod has 18 years of strong, relevant work (design systems, frontend platforms, developer experience, engineering leadership) and almost none of it is public. His domain has said "coming soon" for years. Searching his name mostly shows other Jarod/Jared Taylors, including one he must never be confused with.

He needs one owned home on the web that:
1. tells a recruiter or hiring manager who he is in seconds,
2. proves his design engineering and frontend systems skill instead of just claiming it, and
3. gives him a place to publish writing that LinkedIn and X posts can link to.

## Audience

1. **Recruiters and hiring managers** (primary). Skimming. Need: role, seniority, proof, availability, contact.
2. **Engineering and design leaders / peers.** Reading posts. Need: substance, a reason to follow.
3. **Frontend and design engineers.** Will open dev tools and view source. Need: to be impressed by the craft.

## Positioning

> Designer turned engineer turned engineering leader. For 18 years I've built the work behind the work: design systems, frontend platforms, and developer experience that make whole engineering orgs faster. I've also led the teams that build them, through acquisitions, a bankruptcy, and more reorgs than I can count. These days I'm learning AI the way I learned everything else: hands-on, in public, with an ADHD brain running twenty threads at once.

**Four content pillars:** Leading engineering orgs · Design engineering and frontend systems · Developer experience · Learning AI in public.
**Honesty rule:** AI is framed as *learning in progress*, never as expertise. Don't add claims that aren't in `CONTENT.md`.

## Pages

Should this be a single page site? Homepage and Blog? Or best to have standard pages? If standard pages for growth reasons, initial thoughts:

* Homepage
* About
* Blog
* Work/Projects/Case Studies? A place where I can do case studies because as a leader at 3 different Fortune 500 I've delivered design systems and component libraries. This was done before the industry was even talking about design systems, tokens, etc. I also will have my personal projects/repos (mainly AI or Design System related) so I'm not sure if this belongs on the same page or something separate? 
* Is Contact Me even necessary anymore, or as part of the About Me (and in the footer) I have links to my Email, LinkedIn, Twitter/X, etc? 
* Colophon? This site will be like a portfolio piece, so why not have a page giving the details of how it was designed and built. Very similar to what this guy did: https://aarronwalter.com/colophon

## Ideas for the site

This is not exhaustive. Any new ideas we can come up with should be captured.

### Design System Driven

I'm an engineering leader with more than a decade of experience building Design Systems, Component Libraries, and Teams that build/curate them at Fortune 500 companies (enterprise companies). This site should demonstrate that. 

* **Tokens live in W3C Design Tokens (DTCG) JSON** in the repo, compiled to CSS. This is the source of truth that Figma Variables sync with. Brands should map cleanly to Figma Variable *modes*. Here are some Figma articles:

  * [Design token architecture: Structuring tokens for scale](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/design-token-architecture/)
  * [Design tokens: How to sync design and code in Figma](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/design-tokens/)
* **Design-system components are React (`.tsx`), rendered by Astro.** Pages and layouts stay `.astro`; reusable UI (buttons, tags, cards, nav, section shells, the Remix control) is React so standard `@storybook/react-vite` works with no community plugins.
  - Components render **server-side to static HTML by default** (no `client:*` directive). React ships to the browser only for islands that truly need it, so the zero-JS and Lighthouse targets still hold.
  - Component styles are **plain CSS, Tailwind, or CSS Modules) that consume tokens only**. No CSS-in-JS runtime, no hard-coded values. This keeps the "tokens, not framework" story honest.

## Selected work

**Heading:** A few things I'm proud of.

Featured (first four):

| Metric | Work | Where | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| 29 → 95 Lighthouse performance | Tom Ford Beauty on a new frontend platform | Estée Lauder | Accessibility, Best Practices, and SEO to 100. Feature delivery went from about a month to one sprint. |
| ~7 brands, one design system | Enterprise design system, Figma to tokens to components to CLI | Estée Lauder | Three engineers shipped a production Shopify theme in under a month using only existing components. |
| 1 to 2 days to a new engineer's first PR | Docs hub and internal AI assistant | Estée Lauder | New engineers went from weeks of onboarding to a first PR in one or two days. |
| $1.5B business replatformed | Replatforming during Chapter 11 | JCPenney | Led a 40-person global org on a $6M budget, replatforming a $1.5B eCommerce business. |

Also:

| Work | Where | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Core UI team and design system | JCPenney | Cut feature time-to-market by 50%. |
| CEO-sponsored redesign | JCPenney | Brought 40+ engineers, PMs, and designers together; conversion rose 25% in three months. |
| React component library and CSS framework | Aetna | The docs portal became the single source of truth for frontend teams. |
| Building WellMatch from employee #11 | Aetna | Grew two remote teams to 14 engineers and broke a Rails monolith into microservices. |

## Career

**Heading:** 18 years, one throughline.

| Years | Role | Company |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 to 2026 | Director of Engineering, Core Commerce Capabilities | The Estée Lauder Companies |
| 2021 to 2022 | Director, Digital Engineering | JCPenney |
| 2018 to 2021 | Senior Manager, Digital Engineering | JCPenney |
| 2017 to 2018 | Senior UI Architect | Aetna Digital |
| 2013 to 2017 | Engineering Manager | WellMatch Health (Aetna) |
| 2010 to 2013 | Lead Frontend Engineer | Teladoc |
| 2008 to 2010 | Interface Designer / Frontend Developer | The Dallas Morning News |

## Workbench

**Heading:** The workbench.

**Intro:** Side projects I build by directing AI coding agents. Some of them are paused mid-thought. That's how my brain works, and I'd rather show you the real bench than a polished graveyard.

| Project | Link | Status | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| cadre | https://github.com/jarodtaylor/cadre | v0 works and I use it | A provider-neutral engine for multi-model agent fleets. Hand a task to several specialist agents, each with its own model and tools, then merge what they find. |
| agent-os | https://github.com/jarodtaylor/agent-os | In progress | A local-first control plane and shared brain that lets Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and my other agents work as one team instead of strangers. |
| agent-brain | https://github.com/jarodtaylor/agent-brain | Early | Shared memory across agent tools. Raw notes go in; only reviewed knowledge gets promoted to "truth." |
| agent-cost-tracker | https://github.com/jarodtaylor/agent-cost-tracker | Experiment | A small app for tracking AI tool subscriptions, built as an experiment: planned in Claude Code, built in Codex, QA'd in Cursor, with every rough edge logged. |
| devils-advocate | https://github.com/jarodtaylor/devils-advocate | Paused | A Claude Code plugin that has models from different providers review the same code. |

**Link:** Everything else is on GitHub → https://github.com/jarodtaylor

## Writing

**Heading:** Writing.

**Intro:** First posts are on the way: leadership, design systems, DX, and whatever I'm breaking with AI this week.

**Empty state (no published posts yet):** First posts are on the way. Follow along on LinkedIn in the meantime. *(links to LinkedIn)*

(Once posts exist, this section lists the latest ones automatically.)

## Contact

**Heading:** Let's talk.

**Copy:** I'm open to my next engineering leadership role. I'm also always happy to talk design systems, developer experience, or leading teams through chaos.

**Links:**
- Email: contact@jarodtaylor.com
- LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jarodtaylor
- X: https://x.com/jarodtaylor
- GitHub: https://github.com/jarodtaylor

## Footer

© 2026 Jarod Taylor · Frisco, Texas · Built by hand, with a little help from my agents. View source. *(links to the site repo)*

## Remix control (microcopy, adjustable)

- **Entry point:** Remix this site
- **Panel intro:** Same markup, different tokens. Pick a brand and watch the page change. A nod to CSS Zen Garden, circa 2003.
- **Change readout:** {n} tokens changed · 0 lines of markup changed.
- **v2 teaser:** Coming next: turn the knobs yourself, with a contrast check that won't let you make it unreadable.

content.text:
I've read both docs and the `.impeccable/` folder. One finding before the questions: **you've already done two rounds of Impeccable design exploration**, eight full-page comps in total. Round 1 was Common Ground, Redline, Sunday Edition and Quiet Portfolio. Round 1b was Margin of Possibility, Afterimage, Throughline and Held Together. None were approved. The notes say you rejected round 1 because the layouts looked too alike, and there's no recorded reaction to round 1b.

**Model/effort:** stay on Opus, medium effort, for this interview-style planning. Switch to Fable only for the one-shot synthesis of the final plan and token architecture.
**Plan mode:** once your answers are in and we start writing the plan, enter plan mode.

## Questions that block the plan

Each has my recommendation. Answer "yes" to accept it, or override.

**1. Timeline and phasing.** You've been looking for work since July, and the domain still says "coming soon." That costs you every time a recruiter Googles you.
- **Rec:** Ship in phases. **v0 (~2–3 weeks):** real content, the base brand, the blog, SEO and identity, built on the real token architecture but with one brand. **v1:** Remix with 3 brands. **v2:** Figma Variables and Storybook backfill, plus live knobs.
- Alternative: hold launch until Remix works. That makes a better first impression but means weeks more of "coming soon."

**2. What counts as "tokens only" for Remix.** Your docs pull against each other. Restyling layout and components with 0 lines of markup changed is possible, but it needs a clear boundary.
- **Rec:** In v1, tokens can drive anything CSS can express from custom properties: grid templates, column counts, placement, density, type scale, radius, borders, texture, and showing or hiding decoration. The DOM order never changes. That makes the "0 lines of markup" claim literally true and auditable. Component variant toggles, like flipping the hero layout, come after v1.
- This is the biggest architectural risk, so I want us agreed on it before any design work.

**3. Motion vs. the quality bar.** three.js, reactbits and scroll effects conflict with Lighthouse 100 on mobile and with "works with JS off."
- **Rec:** CSS-first motion (view transitions, scroll-driven animations), with any JS effect added only as progressive enhancement after load. Nothing a recruiter needs depends on it. If a WebGL moment earns its place, it goes in one spot and only on capable devices.
- If they collide, which wins: the Lighthouse 100 claim or the wow?

**4. Page architecture.**
- **Rec:**
  - A **long homepage** that does the recruiter's whole job in one scroll.
  - **/work** for case studies (the Fortune 500 design systems).
  - **/workbench** as a separate page for personal repos. Enterprise outcomes and AI experiments say different things, and mixing them dilutes both.
  - **/writing**.
  - **/about**, which can start as a homepage section and become its own page later.
  - **/colophon**: yes. It's the natural home for the token and Remix story.
  - **No contact page.** Contact goes in the footer and a homepage section.

**5. Previous Impeccable rounds.** Should I treat the 8 comps as input to build on, as sunk cost, or as something to reopen after planning? Did anything in round 1b land for you, even a piece of one?

## Gaps you're likely missing

**6. Recruiter conversion.** CONTENT.md has nothing on:
- the target role and level (Director? VP? Head of?)
- remote, hybrid or relocation stance
- a downloadable résumé PDF
- testimonials or recommendations, even 2–3 LinkedIn quotes

**Rec:** include all four. Recruiters filter on level and location before anything else.

**7. Case study content doesn't exist yet.** CONTENT.md has one-line outcomes. Real case studies need the context, the constraints, what you did and the results.
- **Rec:** add a structured career interview as an explicit phase. I interview you, about 3 sessions, and draft 2–3 case studies plus a sharper About.
- Which companies' work can you legally show (screenshots, internal names), and what has to stay vague?

**8. Writing at launch.** An empty blog undercuts "a place to publish."
- **Rec:** launch with 1–2 posts. The obvious first one is the meta post: building a Zen Garden–style site with DTCG tokens. It doubles as the Colophon's long form and as your first LinkedIn post.
- Do you have any drafts or topics already in mind?

**9. Telling you apart from other Jarod Taylors.** Person JSON-LD helps search engines. Humans need a visible cue.
- **Rec:** a real headshot, and your full name and location prominent in the hero.
- Do you have a recent photo? Any problem with putting it on the site?

**10. Nord as the base brand.** I'd push back. Nord is one of the most recognizable dev-tool palettes, so it reads as "VS Code theme," which works against "fresh, not slop." Several of its standard pairings, like the muted grays on the dark backgrounds and the frost blues on the light ones, likely fail AA (I'll check with a script).
- **Rec:** use Nord as a *mood* (cool, calm, Nordic restraint), not as literal hex values. One Remix brand could be a faithful Nord homage.
- Did you mean Nord literally, or the feeling?

**11. Inspiration sites.** For each of the 5 sites, which part did you bookmark it for?
- **Rec:** walk them together during the design phase, not now. I'll drive a real browser and you narrate.

**12. Remix as a recruiter feature, not just a dev toy.** A recruiter won't care about tokens, but a hiring manager for a design systems or platform role will.
- **Rec:** add a short "What you just saw" explainer that maps Remix to the business value: "this is how one system served ~7 Estée Lauder brands." That turns the demo into proof of the ~7-brand claim.
- Agree?

**13. Other gaps I'd add to the plan unless you object:**
- an RSS feed
- auto-generated OG images per post, rendered from the active brand's tokens (your exportable-tokens idea, made real)
- a newsletter or follow option (or explicitly not)
- a /now or /uses page
- a "speaking / available to talk" line
- a 404 page that shows off Remix

## Housekeeping (no answer needed)

- There's no git repo, no project CLAUDE.md and no `tasks/lessons.md` yet. I'll set those up when we move to building.
- The Impeccable comparison server from the last round is dead.

Answer however your brain wants: a numbered list, a ramble, or a voice-memo transcript all work. I'll turn your answers into the plan.

Okay, so we can ditch the old impeccable stuff. They were all failures. I was trying to do the Comp first approach as opposed to just designing with code and they all just really missed the mark. So, we can scratch those and start fresh. Yes, ship in phases is fine. No point in giving timelines (2-3 weeks) because let's be honest, agents work way faster than humans. As for the Remix. I agree. We can start with simple token/css changes and punt the idea of layout rendering (e.g. hero changes) for now. This might be a solid experiment later with the site which I can document and capture for another blog post. Motion stuff... the idea here is not to have just a boring static page. I want something that has some "wow" to it but without shredding our Lighthouse and performance. As for the "no js", I'm not stuck on that. That was from a previous session that the agent added. You can do these things and still have great performance, but it has to be done right. I'm also not a stickler for the Lighthouse has to be 100. Of course I don't want it to be crap, but we can weigh the pros and cons between "wow" and perf degradation. Good with the page architecture. As for the recruiter conversion. I don't agree that I need to have my desired role, desired location, etc. on this. That's what LinkedIn is for. I do agree that a downloadable resume makes sense. Testimonials, yes! I actually thought I captured that somewhere, but must have missed it. I have previous leaders (VPs, Exec Directors, CTO, etc) that would definitely give a quote. Case studies don't exist yet. I will have to work on those separately. The goal right now is to nail down the design, architecture, etc. The content can come as it comes. As for a headshot... I think I'm okay with this IF it doesn't take away from the design of the homepage. I kind of find it a little cheesy when people have a big image of themselves on the top of the homepage/hero. Definitely can do a few of these for the About section or page, though. My desire first is a sexy design and unique experience (with the remixing, etc). As for the the theme, I'm totally fine with ditching Nord. I had just previously told an agent that I tend to love the Catpuccin, Nord, Dracula, etc. themes. We can work on the brand/colors. Good with your other ideas/gaps you found.

## 1. DTCG spec status
- **Stable.** The Format Module 2025.10 and the Resolver Module 2025.10 were both published as W3C Community Group final reports on 2025-10-28. Each says "This specification is considered stable." (The drafts on designtokens.org still carry a "preview" warning, but they are the drafts, not the final versions.)
- **Format 2025.10 covers what you need:** aliases (`{group.token}`), group inheritance via `$extends`, and colours as objects (`colorSpace`, `components`, `alpha`, optional `hex`).
- **Resolver = multi-brand.** You define sets and modifiers, for example a `brand` modifier, and the result is one token set per combination (the spec calls these "permutations"). There's an official JSON Schema and a playground (added Dec 2025).
- Sources: https://www.w3.org/community/reports/design-tokens/CG-FINAL-format-20251028/ · https://www.w3.org/community/reports/design-tokens/CG-FINAL-resolver-20251028/ · https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/
- **Recommendation:** Write tokens in 2025.10 format and use a resolver file with a `brand` modifier (plus a `scheme` modifier if you want light/dark).

## 2. Token build tools
- **Terrazzo `@terrazzo/cli` 2.8.0** (released 2026-10-13; 2.0.0 came out 2026-03-17):
  - 2.0 added full 2025.10 support, including resolvers. It errors on the older draft format, so colours and dimensions must be objects.
  - The CSS plugin takes a `permutations: [{ input: { brand: "x" }, prepare: (c) => \`[data-brand="x"] { ${c} }\` }]` option. All brands end up in one CSS file, wrapped in whatever selectors you write.
  - It can also limit each output block to certain sets or modifiers, and it warns when your modifiers overlap (the docs call this a "non-orthogonal" resolver).
  - The old Terrazzo-only "modes" still work (`modeSelectors`), but the docs call resolvers their successor.
  - It has a built-in Figma importer. As of 2.8.0 it keeps each variable's key so tokens still match after you republish the library.
  - Sources: https://terrazzo.app/docs/integrations/css/ · https://terrazzo.app/docs/guides/resolvers/ · https://raw.githubusercontent.com/terrazzoapp/terrazzo/main/packages/cli/CHANGELOG.md
- **Style Dictionary 5.6.1** (released 2026-10-10; 5.0.0 came out 2025-05):
  - **2025.10 support is partial.** Colour objects landed in 5.3.0 (all 14 colour spaces, OKLCH output). Dimension objects landed in 5.4.0, and border/shadow updates in 5.3.1.
  - Issue #1590 is still open: the resolver isn't implemented and no PR exists (design discussion as of 2026-10-12). `$extends` isn't tracked there, and gradient and duration are still in progress.
  - Multi-brand works by looping: you create one `StyleDictionary` instance per brand with different `source` globs.
  - The `css/variables` format takes a `selector` option (string or array), so `[data-brand="x"]` is possible, but you have to set up the brand loop yourself.
  - Sources: https://github.com/style-dictionary/style-dictionary/issues/1590 · https://raw.githubusercontent.com/style-dictionary/style-dictionary/main/CHANGELOG.md · Context7 `/style-dictionary/style-dictionary` (multi-brand-multi-platform example)
- **Recommendation:** Use Terrazzo. It's the only one that reads 2025.10 resolver files natively and outputs per-brand `[data-brand]` blocks from config alone.

## 3. Figma Variables and DTCG
- **Correction:** Native import/export was announced at Figma Schema 2025 (Nov 2025), not at Config. Forum users report it reaching accounts gradually from early Dec 2025.
- **What Figma's help docs say:**
  - Import: drag DTCG JSON into a collection. Each file becomes one mode. A variable is only created if the token is in every file with the same `$type`.
  - Export: right-click a mode and choose "Export mode", or right-click the collection and choose "Export modes".
- **Import limits:**
  - Colours must be HSL or sRGB, so OKLCH or P3 tokens won't import cleanly.
  - Dimensions must be px; durations must be in seconds.
  - Font family must be a single string, not an array.
  - Booleans need the `com.figma.type` extension.
  - Typography and other composite tokens aren't supported.
  - Names are flattened to slash paths.

- **Plans** (from Figma's plans page):

  | Plan | Modes per collection |
  |---|---|
  | Starter | None (so "modes = brands" doesn't work) |
  | Professional | Up to 10 |
  | Organization | Up to 20 |
  | Enterprise | Unlimited, plus extended collections |

- **Variables REST API:** requires a full seat in an Enterprise org. Reading needs `file_variables:read`; writing needs an admin. Terrazzo's Figma variable import uses this API, so it is Enterprise-only too.
- **Alternatives:** Tokens Studio, which turns each mode into a token set (https://docs.tokens.studio/figma/import/variables/), or community plugins.
- Sources: https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/15343816063383-Modes-for-variables · https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040328273-Figma-plans-and-features · https://developers.figma.com/docs/rest-api/variables/ · https://forum.figma.com/ask-the-community-7/native-variable-export-feature-47831
- **Recommendation:** Treat the repo JSON as the source of truth and use native import/export on the Professional plan.
  - Keep a parallel sRGB colour value for Figma if you write OKLCH.
  - Keep typography as separate token types in code only.
  - Don't plan around the REST API unless you're on Enterprise.

- **Astro 7.3.8 is current** (7.0.0 released 2026-06-22; 6.0.0 released 2026-03-10).
- **What changed in 7:**
  - Vite 8 and a Rust compiler (stricter HTML: unclosed tags are now errors).
  - The default Markdown processor no longer runs remark/rehype plugins; you have to opt back in.
  - `compressHTML` now defaults to `'jsx'`, which can remove whitespace between inline elements.
  - Some `astro:transitions` internal helpers were removed.
  - `getContainerRenderer()` moved to a `/container-renderer` import.
- **`@astrojs/react` 7.0.1** supports React 17, 18 and 19, and is fine for server-rendered `.tsx` plus islands.
- **Content collections:** defined in `src/content.config.ts` with the `glob()`/`file()` loaders. Live collections (fetched at request time, in `src/live.config.ts`) need an adapter.
- **View transitions:** `<ClientRouter />` isn't deprecated, but the docs say it "will increasingly become unnecessary" now that browsers support native cross-document transitions.
- **Cloudflare:** a fully static site doesn't need the adapter. You need a `wrangler.jsonc` with `assets.directory: "./dist"`, and `not_found_handling: "404-page"` if you want a custom 404 page. `@astrojs/cloudflare` 14.3.4 is only for server rendering.
- **Storybook for Astro:** I found no official first-party framework, only a community one (`@storybook-astro/renderer` 1.7.x).
- Sources: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/upgrade-to/v7/ · https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/view-transitions/ · https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/content-collections/ · https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/cloudflare/
- **Recommendation:** Astro 7 with React components rendered on the server, native cross-document view transitions rather than ClientRouter, and `@storybook/react-vite` for the `.tsx` components.

## 5. Storybook
- **Storybook 10.6.2 is current** (10.0 released 2025-10-28). It is ESM-only and supports Vite 8. Use `@storybook/react-vite`.
- **Brand switching:**
  - `@storybook/addon-themes` 10.6.2 provides `withThemeByDataAttribute({ themes, defaultTheme, attributeName: 'data-brand', parentSelector: 'html' })`. It handles one setting per decorator.

  - A story can pin its brand with `globals: { brand: 'x' }`.
- Sources: https://storybook.js.org/docs/essentials/toolbars-and-globals · https://raw.githubusercontent.com/storybookjs/storybook/next/code/addons/themes/docs/api.md
- **Recommendation:** Use addon-themes with `attributeName: 'data-brand'`, and add a small custom toolbar entry if you need a second setting.

| Feature | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `color-mix()` | Baseline, widely available | Fully supported since 2025-11 |
| `oklab()` / `oklch()` | Baseline, widely available | Fully supported since 2025-11 |

- **Recommendation:** Build the brand-swap core on the supported features (custom properties, OKLCH, relative colour, `color-mix()`, `@property`, style queries). - Cloudflare's own Pages docs now say "Start new projects with Workers" in a callout titled "Are you sure you want to use Pages?". It calls Workers its main application platform with a broader feature set. Astro's deploy guide says the same.

# jarodtaylor.com: master plan

## Context

Jarod has 18 years of design systems, frontend platform, DX and engineering leadership work, and almost none of it is public. The domain says "coming soon," and he is mid job search, so every week without a site costs him.

The site has three jobs:
1. Tell a recruiter who he is in seconds.
2. Prove his design engineering craft instead of claiming it.
3. Host writing that LinkedIn and X posts can link to.

The signature feature is **Remix**: same markup, different tokens, completely different brand. It's a modern CSS Zen Garden. It's portfolio proof of the "~7 brands, one design system" claim, and the token pipeline runs Figma → DTCG → build → Storybook → site.

**Already decided:**
- Ship in phases.
- Remix v1 is token/CSS only. Component layout variants are a later experiment and a later blog post.
- Wow is wanted. Perf is a budget to spend wisely, not a perfect Lighthouse 100, and JS is fine when it's done right.
- No target role, level or location on the site. That's LinkedIn's job.
- Résumé PDF and testimonials are in.
- No hero headshot. Photos go in About.
- Brand colors get designed fresh, not taken from Nord.
- Design happens in code, not comp-first. Old Impeccable rounds are scrapped.
- Case-study content comes later. This plan nails design and architecture.

Lessons from this session are in `tasks/lessons.md`.

---

## Stack (verified against current docs, 2026-10-13)

| Layer | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Site | **Astro 7** static output, `@astrojs/react`. Pages and layouts are `.astro`. Design-system components are `.tsx`, rendered on the server. Islands only for Remix and any motion that needs JS. | Zero JS by default and clean HTML. React components give Storybook a first-class path. |
| Tokens | **W3C DTCG 2025.10** format plus the **Resolver module** (a `brand` modifier). | Both have been stable W3C CG reports since 2025-10-28. The resolver *is* the multi-brand spec. |
| Token build | **Terrazzo** (`@terrazzo/cli` 2.x). The CSS plugin uses `permutations` to emit `[data-brand="x"]` blocks. | It's the only tool with native support for 2025.10 resolvers. Style Dictionary 5.6 still has no resolver support (issue #1590 is open). |
| Styling | **Plain CSS**: cascade layers (`reset, tokens, base, components, utilities`), co-located per component, readable class names, consuming **only** component and semantic custom properties. No Tailwind, no CSS Modules hashes. | View-source is part of the portfolio. "Tokens, not framework" stays literally true. *(Override if you want Tailwind v4.)* |
| Components workshop | **Storybook 10** + `@storybook/react-vite` + `@storybook/addon-themes` (`withThemeByDataAttribute`, `attributeName: 'data-brand'`). | It's the standard path, and the brand toolbar comes from config alone. |
| Figma | Repo JSON is the **source of truth**. Figma Variables get it through **native DTCG import/export**, one mode per brand. | Native import shipped in late 2025. The REST API is Enterprise-only, so skip it. |
| Hosting | **Cloudflare Workers static assets** (`wrangler.jsonc`, `assets.directory: ./dist`, `not_found_handling: "404-page"`). Cloudflare Web Analytics. Email Routing for `contact@`. | Cloudflare now steers new projects to Workers over Pages. Static requests are free. |
| Content | Astro content collections: `posts` (MDX), `work`, `workbench`, `career`, `testimonials`, `pillars`. | One data source feeds the homepage, the pages, the résumé, RSS and JSON-LD. |

**Figma constraints to design around:**
- Native import accepts only sRGB/HSL colors, px dimensions and single-string font families. It doesn't take typography composites.
- Fix: the build emits a **Figma-flavored export** (sRGB fallbacks, flattened type tokens) next to the OKLCH CSS.
- Modes need the **Figma Professional plan or higher**.

---

## Token architecture (the core decision)

Three tiers, visible in the repo:

```
tokens/
  knobs/                 # TIER 1: the only thing a brand authors
    default.json         #   hue/chroma anchors, base size, scale ratio, density,
    <alt-1>.json         #   radius, border weight, font families, texture, motion personality
    <alt-2>.json
  generated/<brand>.json # TIER 1b: derived primitives (color ramps, type scale, space scale), never hand-edited
  semantic/*.json        # TIER 2: aliases → surface roles (surface, surface-inverse, surface-accent,
                         #   text-*, border-*), space steps, type steps, motion
  component/*.json       # TIER 3: what components consume (button.*, card.*, nav.*, section.*)
  resolver.json          # DTCG resolver: modifier "brand" → knobs + generated set per brand
scripts/derive.ts        # pure function: derive(knobs) → primitive tokens (DTCG JSON)
terrazzo.config.ts       # → src/styles/tokens.css  ([data-brand] blocks) + dist/tokens/<brand>.json
```

**Key move: derivation is one pure TS function, `derive(knobs)`.**
- DTCG aliases can't do math. Scales and ramps need math, and Figma can't do math either.
- So `derive.ts` turns knobs into concrete primitive tokens **at build time**. Terrazzo then compiles those, and Figma imports real values.
- The **same function** runs in the browser for **Remix v2 live knobs**. v2 becomes "call `derive()` and set custom properties." No second implementation and no refactor.
- Color is derived in **OKLCH**, with sRGB fallbacks emitted for Figma.

**compressHTML**
- Type: `boolean | "jsx"`
- Default: `'jsx'`
- "Since v7.0, Astro applies by default the JSX whitespace rules used by frameworks like React."
- `true` removes whitespace from `.astro` components in a lossless manner.

**build.inlineStylesheets**
- Type: `'always' | 'auto' | 'never'`
- Default: `auto`
- `'always'`: "project styles are inlined into `<style>` tags"

- `'never'`: project styles are sent in external stylesheets.

**scopedStyleStrategy**
- Type: `'where' | 'class' | 'attribute'`
- Default: `'attribute'`
- `'where'`: uses `:where` selectors, adding no specificity.
- `'class'`: uses class-based selectors, adding +1 specificity.
- `'attribute'`: uses `data-` attributes, adding +1 specificity.

- Résumé PDF and testimonials are in.
- No hero headshot. Photos go in About.
- Brand colors get designed fresh, not taken from Nord.
- Design happens in code, not comp-first. Old Impeccable rounds are scrapped.
- Case-study content comes later. This plan nails design and architecture.

## Stack (verified against current docs, 2026-10-13)

| Layer | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Site | **Astro 7** static output, `@astrojs/react`. Pages and layouts are `.astro`. Design-system components are `.tsx`, rendered on the server. Islands only for Remix and any motion that needs JS. | Zero JS by default and clean HTML. React components give Storybook a first-class path. |
| Tokens | **W3C DTCG 2025.10** format plus the **Resolver module** (a `brand` modifier). | Both have been stable W3C CG reports since 2025-10-28. The resolver *is* the multi-brand spec. |
| Token build | **Terrazzo** (`@terrazzo/cli` 2.x). The CSS plugin uses `permutations` to emit `[data-brand="x"]` blocks. | It's the only tool with native support for 2025.10 resolvers. Style Dictionary 5.6 still has no resolver support (issue #1590 is open). |
| Styling | **Plain CSS**: cascade layers (`reset, tokens, base, components, utilities`), co-located per component, readable class names, consuming **only** component and semantic custom properties. No Tailwind, no CSS Modules hashes. | View-source is part of the portfolio. "Tokens, not framework" stays literally true. *(Override if you want Tailwind v4.)* |
| Components workshop | **Storybook 10** + `@storybook/react-vite` + `@storybook/addon-themes` (`withThemeByDataAttribute`, `attributeName: 'data-brand'`). | It's the standard path, and the brand toolbar comes from config alone. |
| Figma | Repo JSON is the **source of truth**. Figma Variables get it through **native DTCG import/export**, one mode per brand. | Native import shipped in late 2025. The REST API is Enterprise-only, so skip it. |
| Hosting | **Cloudflare Workers static assets** (`wrangler.jsonc`, `assets.directory: ./dist`, `not_found_handling: "404-page"`). Cloudflare Web Analytics. Email Routing for `contact@`. | Cloudflare now steers new projects to Workers over Pages. Static requests are free. |

- Native import accepts only sRGB/HSL colors, px dimensions and single-string font families. It doesn't take typography composites.

## Token architecture (the core decision)

Three tiers, visible in the repo:

```
tokens/
  knobs/                 # TIER 1: the only thing a brand authors
    default.json         #   hue/chroma anchors, base size, scale ratio, density,
    <alt-1>.json         #   radius, border weight, font families, texture, motion personality
    <alt-2>.json
  generated/<brand>.json # TIER 1b: derived primitives (color ramps, type scale, space scale), never hand-edited
  semantic/*.json        # TIER 2: aliases → surface roles (surface, surface-inverse, surface-accent,
                         #   text-*, border-*), space steps, type steps, motion
  component/*.json       # TIER 3: what components consume (button.*, card.*, nav.*, section.*)
  resolver.json          # DTCG resolver: modifier "brand" → knobs + generated set per brand
scripts/derive.ts        # pure function: derive(knobs) → primitive tokens (DTCG JSON)
terrazzo.config.ts       # → src/styles/tokens.css  ([data-brand] blocks) + dist/tokens/<brand>.json
```

**Key move: derivation is one pure TS function, `derive(knobs)`.**
- DTCG aliases can't do math. Scales and ramps need math, and Figma can't do math either.
- So `derive.ts` turns knobs into concrete primitive tokens **at build time**. Terrazzo then compiles those, and Figma imports real values.
- The **same function** runs in the browser for **Remix v2 live knobs**. v2 becomes "call `derive()` and set custom properties." No second implementation and no refactor.
- Color is derived in **OKLCH**, with sRGB fallbacks emitted for Figma.

**Phase 0 spike: alias output.**
- Remix v2 needs the semantic and component tiers to come out as `var(--primitive)` references. If they're flattened to values, setting a primitive at runtime changes nothing downstream.
- Terrazzo's CSS docs don't say which it does.
- **Spike it first.** If it flattens, fall back to a small custom Terrazzo plugin, or emit the semantic and component layers ourselves from the resolved alias graph.

**Brands can differ in more than color:**
- Typography family and scale, spacing density, radius, border weight, texture or decoration.
- Grid templates and column counts through custom properties, plus decoration shown or hidden.
- **DOM order never changes.**
- Discrete layout and decoration choices are **enumerated knob tokens**, e.g. `--hero-layout: split | stacked` and `--decoration: rules | none`. Component CSS reacts to them with **container style queries**, Baseline since 2026-05.
- **Never key CSS on a brand's name.** No per-brand CSS anywhere, so the "{n} tokens changed" readout is the whole truth.
- Gotcha: a style query only styles *descendants* of the element that carries the property.
- Progressive extras go behind `@supports`.

**View-source cleanliness (Astro defaults work against it):**
- `compressHTML: false`. Astro 7's default `'jsx'` collapses whitespace.
- `scopedStyleStrategy: 'where'`, or better, no scoped `<style>` in `.astro` files at all. Component CSS lives in plain co-located `.css` files.
- `build.inlineStylesheets: 'never'`.
- Turn off Vite CSS minification (`vite.build.cssMinify`; check the exact value on vite.dev) and serve readable CSS. Gzip/brotli makes the size cost negligible.
- Hashed CSS filenames are fine and get cache headers. The *contents* are what people read.

**Fonts:**
- The default brand's fonts are self-hosted, subset, preloaded and fallback-metric-matched, so there's no layout shift.
- Alternate brand fonts load **only when that brand is activated**, so Remix costs the first paint nothing.

**Two plan changes this forces:**

2. **Email authentication gap.** There's no SPF record and no DMARC record. Your mail from `contact@` is more likely to land in spam, which hurts mid job search. Adding SPF, Google's DKIM key and a DMARC record is a quick fix and worth doing whatever we decide on hosting.

**Hosting decision:**

| Option | What it means | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Move DNS to Cloudflare, host on Workers** *(rec)* | Add the domain to Cloudflare, copy the Route 53 records (Google MX included), then change the nameservers at DreamHost. | Preview deploys per branch, free static hosting, Web Analytics with no cookie banner, and the Cloudflare MCP can manage it all. | B. Stay on AWS | Use S3 + CloudFront, which you already have. | No migration, but preview deploys, analytics and cache invalidation all become our own CI code. Workers can't serve this domain unless DNS moves to Cloudflare. |

I recommend **A**. It matches the plan and removes the most ongoing work. The switch carries little risk if we copy every record first and check MX before changing nameservers. Pick B if you'd rather keep everything on AWS.

|-----|----------|---------------|-------------|

## 2. Triage: Separate New from Pending

Before processing, reconcile the reply and resolution state of each piece of feedback.

**Review threads**: An ordinarily handled thread is complete only when it has both a visible, submitted substantive reply and authoritative thread resolution. Reconcile those conditions independently:

- A reply that explicitly defers a human choice (e.g., "need to align on this", "going to think through this", or options without a decision) is a **pending decision**. Keep the thread open and do not re-process it.
- A reply that records a completed fix or reply verdict while the thread is still open is **resolution-pending**. Do not repost the reply or reapply the fix; carry the existing visible reply to step 7 and complete only the missing resolution after pending-review state is empty.
- A thread without either kind of substantive response is **new**.

**PR comments and review bodies**: These have no resolve mechanism, so they reappear on every run. Apply two filters in order:

1. **Actionability**: An item is actionable when it is someone's open request to this PR: something to fix, answer, or decide. This filter is also what keeps the run from looping on its own output. A reply posted by this run or an earlier one is a record of handling, not a request, so it drops here, whether it reports a fix or carries a parked `needs-human` decision. That parked item is already tracked as itself; re-reading its own write-up as fresh feedback is how the loop would never settle. Who posted an item never decides this, including the account that opened the PR. Examples: review wrapper text ("Here are some automated review suggestions..."), approvals ("this looks great!"), status badges ("Validated"), CI summaries with no follow-up asks. If there's nothing to fix, answer, or decide, it's not actionable -- drop it from the count entirely.
2. **Already replied**: For actionable items, check the PR conversation for an existing reply that quotes and addresses the feedback. If a reply already exists, skip. If not, it's new.

The distinction is about content, not who posted what. A deferral from a teammate, a previous skill run, or a manual reply all count. Similarly, actionability is about content -- bot feedback that requests a specific code change is actionable; a bot's boilerplate header wrapping those requests is not.

**Silent drop.** Non-actionable items are dropped without narration. Do not announce, list, or count dropped items in conversation, the task list, or the step 9 summary. Review-bot wrappers from CodeRabbit, Codex, Gemini Code Assist, and Copilot (bodies like "Here are some automated review suggestions...") commonly appear here -- recognize them by their boilerplate content, drop silently. The fetch script filters out only blank bodies. Every author and every kind of feedback — the PR author, CI/status bots such as Codecov, review bots — goes through this content check, so a reused account or a changed format cannot silently hide actionable feedback.

If there are no new or resolution-pending items across all feedback types, skip steps 3-8 and go straight to step 9. If only resolution-pending threads remain, skip steps 3-6 and go straight to step 7.

## 3. Consolidate & Decide (the legitimacy gate)

This is where validity is decided. Judge every **new** item here, in your own context, before any fix is dispatched. Apply the rubric in [references/evaluation-rubric.md](evaluation-rubric.md) (read it now) across the whole batch at once. When the invocation carries a `trajectory`, apply the non-convergence test in [references/pipeline-mode.md](pipeline-mode.md) before dispatching anything — a demonstrated shared root is answered once, at the root, instead of fixing each instance.

Working over the full set lets you do what a per-thread subagent can't:
- **Dedup reads by file** — read a file once and judge all its threads together.
- **Cross-item reasoning** — cluster findings by root assumption; a source (often a bot) that's wrong in one place is suspect across its siblings; converging requests from independent reviewers are a strong fix signal.
- **Selective depth** — clear nits need only the comment plus the diff line; deep-read (callers, invariants, `git blame`/PR rationale for author intent) only where a finding is contestable or the code looks deliberate. That deep read on the contestable minority is what catches a confidently-wrong reviewer.

Produce a verdict per item and sort into three lists:

- **fix-list** — `fixed` / `fixed-differently`. These get dispatched to fixers in step 4. For each, note the file/location (and for outdated threads, the resolved location or anchor) and a one-line "what to change." **Class fix:** when the cross-item pass (rubric: "A validated finding can span sites this PR itself introduced") found equivalent same-invariant sites this PR touched, record them as **one** fix-list item that enumerates every concrete location (`file:line`) and lists every feedback ID it covers — one class item → one fixer (step 4), so the sites are edited coherently and every covered thread/comment is replied-to and resolved from that single result. Enumerate only sites whose treatment is unambiguous; a site needing its own judgment stays a separate item.
- **reply-list** — `replied` / `not-addressing` / `declined`. No code change. Compose the reply text now per the rubric (you have the evidence) and carry it to step 7.
- **human-list** — `needs-human`. Compose `decision_context` now and run the rubric's "Adjudicate before escalating" step on each judgment-bound item; an adjudicated verdict moves the item to the list it names, and the rest carry to steps 7 and 9.

Create a task list of all new items (e.g., `TaskCreate` in Claude Code, `update_plan` in Codex) tagged with their verdict, so progress is visible.

**At scale.** If the batch is large (many threads spanning many files) and judging them all inline would overflow your context, process the consolidation in groups (e.g., file-clustered groups of ~8-10 threads), emitting the three lists incrementally. Don't fan the judgment out to subagents to avoid this — batch it instead.

If the fix-list is empty (all verdicts are reply/needs-human), skip steps 4-6 and go to step 7.

## 4. Fix (fix-list only)

Dispatch fixers **only** for fix-list items. Reply-list and human-list items never reach a subagent.

### Where each fix runs

Step 3 already read the code behind every fix-list item. Dispatch fixers when the items form a real parallel batch (two or more items on disjoint files), or for an item whose fix reaches well beyond what you read (a rename across callers, a class fix over many sites). Apply every other item in this context, with the fixer prompt below as your own instructions.

Every fix-list item ends with one **per-item result** in the return format below, whether a fixer produced it or you did. The **change set** for this run is the union of those results' `files_changed`. Steps 5-7 read only per-item results and the change set, never which path produced them.

### Dispatch

Read [references/agents/pr-comment-resolver.md](agents/pr-comment-resolver.md) and spawn a generic subagent seeded with that fixer prompt for each fix-list item you are delegating. Do not dispatch a standalone agent by type/name. The fixer only implements: the validity judgment is already done, so it implements and returns; it does not re-judge whether the fix is worthwhile.

Each fixer receives:
- The feedback_id (thread ID or comment ID) and feedback type.
- The file path and location fields: `line`, `originalLine`, `startLine`, `originalStartLine` (for outdated threads, the resolved location/anchor from step 3).
- The reviewer's comment text.
- Your step-3 note: what to change and why it was judged valid.
- The PR number.

For `pr_comment` / `review_body` fix-list items (no file/line), the fixer identifies the relevant files from the comment text and the PR diff.

**No subagent capability — apply the fixes yourself, sequentially.** When the harness exposes no way to dispatch (or a dispatch fails), work the fix-list in this context one item at a time, using the fixer prompt as your own instructions and producing the same per-item result. This is a supported path, not a shortfall to report as lost coverage: the decision about whether each item is valid already happened in step 3, and fixers only *implement* changes you approved, so running them here costs parallelism and context headroom — never correctness. Keep the dispatch path's discipline: one item at a time, re-read each file before editing it, and stop to re-evaluate if implementing reveals a contradiction (the `blocked` handling applies unchanged). Items you apply in this context by choice follow the same discipline.

This skill therefore does not depend on agent-tool authorization to complete a review. That is deliberate: it runs unattended under `ce-babysit-pr`, where a permission prompt would stall the whole loop, so it needs few tools and can still fix without dispatch.

### Per-item result format (fixer or inline)

- **verdict**: `fixed`, `fixed-differently`, or `blocked`
- **feedback_id**, **feedback_type**
- **reply_text**: markdown reply to post (quoting the relevant feedback) — omit for `blocked`
- **files_changed**: list of files modified (empty for `blocked`)
- **reason**: what was done, or the concrete contradiction for `blocked`

**Handling `blocked`.** A fixer returns `blocked` only when implementing revealed a concrete contradiction that the fixer could see and you could not (the change breaks a caller/test it can see, or the code isn't what the finding described). Re-evaluate it yourself with that evidence: either re-dispatch with a corrected instruction, or move it to the reply-list (`not-addressing`/`declined`) or human-list. Don't silently drop it.

### Batching and conflict avoidance

**Batching**: If 1-4 items are delegated, dispatch them all in parallel. For 5+, batch in groups of 4.

**Conflict avoidance**: No two fixers that touch the same file run in parallel. You already know the target files from step 3 — serialize fixers that share a file (dispatch one, wait, then the next); non-overlapping items run in parallel. For a **class item**, feed the fixer its full enumerated location set and every covered feedback ID (not a single thread), and account for **all** of its sites in this check — a class fix touching files another fixer also touches must be serialized against every one of them. When one fixer handles multiple threads on the same file, it addresses them sequentially.

**Sequential fallback**: Platforms that do not support parallel dispatch run fixers sequentially.

Fixes can occasionally expand beyond their referenced file (e.g., renaming a method updates callers elsewhere). This is rare but can cause parallel fixers to collide. Step 5 (combined validation) catches test breakage; step 8 (verify) catches unresolved threads. If either reveals inconsistent changes, re-run the affected fixers sequentially.

## 5. Validate Combined State

If the change set is empty, skip steps 5 and 6 and proceed to step 7.

Each fix runs only targeted tests on its own change. This step runs the project's full validation **once** against the combined diff to catch interactions between fixes that targeted runs can't see.

1. **Run the project's validation command** (test suite, type check, or whatever the project's active conventions specify). Run once, not per-agent.

2. **Green** -> proceed to step 6.

3. **Red, failures touch files in the change set** -> one inline diagnose-and-fix pass. Re-run validation. If still red, escalate with a `needs-human` item containing the test output; do **not** commit.

4. **Red, failures touch only files outside the change set** -> treat as pre-existing. Proceed to step 6, but add a footer to the commit message: `Note: pre-existing failure in <test> not addressed by this PR.`

Record the validation outcome (command run, pass/fail counts, any pre-existing failures noted) for the step 9 summary.

## 6. Commit and Publication

Commit only the change set, preserving unrelated work in the tree and index, with a message referencing the PR:

```bash
git add [files in the change set]
git commit -m "Address PR review feedback (#PR_NUMBER)

- [list changes from per-item results]" -- [files in the change set]
```

In `mode:return-to-caller`, capture the combined fix commit SHA and follow [references/return-to-caller.md](return-to-caller.md) to save every judged action and intended checklist tick. Return after saving; do not push or enter steps 7-8 for any part of this batch. A failed commit or save reports the actual local state and incomplete handoff, never completion.

Ordinary and pipeline execution publish the commit before the remote tail:
```bash

```

## 7. Reply and Resolve

Enter the remote tail only when the batch's fix commit is published, or the batch created no code changes. Return-to-caller batches with a fix stop at step 6; their saved reply-only and human-list items remain deferred too. No-change return-to-caller batches use this existing protocol and save observed progress even when a write fails. Resume enters here only through the publication and reconciliation conditions in [references/resume.md](resume.md), uses the saved verdicts and exact reply bodies, and returns there after completing or stopping the remote tail. Apply eligible PR checklist ticks under the entrypoint's publication condition.

The done condition for an ordinary review thread is one visible, submitted substantive reply plus authoritative resolution; satisfy each condition independently and never repeat a satisfied half. Post for every newly handled item: fix-list items use the `reply_text` from their per-item result; reply-list and human-list items use the reply text you composed in step 3. A **class item** carries multiple covered feedback IDs (`feedback_ids`/`feedback_types` from its fixer) — reply to and resolve *every* one, posting the shared `reply_text` on each thread, not just the first; a covered thread left unresolved shows up as new work again in the next `ce-babysit-pr` loop. The mechanism depends on the feedback type.

### Reply format

All replies quote the relevant part of the original feedback for continuity — the specific sentence or passage, not the entire comment if it's long. The per-verdict templates are in [references/evaluation-rubric.md](evaluation-rubric.md) (skip verdicts) and [references/agents/pr-comment-resolver.md](agents/pr-comment-resolver.md) (`fixed` / `fixed-differently`).

For `needs-human` verdicts, post the natural-sounding reply but do NOT resolve the thread. Leave it open for human input.

### Review threads

For every calling mode, select the first unsatisfied completion condition before acting. A thread with no visible submitted substantive reply runs steps 0-4. A `resolution-pending` thread skips only step 1, uses its existing reply IDs for step 2, and runs steps 2-4; do not judge, fix, or post again. A `needs-human` thread stops after its visible submitted reply and remains unresolved.

Current GitHub state decides independently of local progress. A POST may succeed before the helper's pending-review check fails or before a checkpoint is written. # agent-browser core

Fast browser automation CLI for AI agents. Chrome/Chromium via CDP, no Playwright or Puppeteer dependency. Accessibility-tree snapshots with compact `@eN` refs let agents interact with pages in ~200-400 tokens instead of parsing raw HTML.

Most normal web tasks (navigate, read, click, fill, extract, screenshot) are covered here. Load a specialized skill when the task falls outside browser web pages — see [When to load another skill](#when-to-load-another-skill).

## The core loop

```bash
agent-browser open <url>        # 1. Open a page
agent-browser snapshot -i       # 2. See what's on it (interactive elements only)
agent-browser click @e3         # 3. Act on refs from the snapshot
agent-browser snapshot -i       # 4. Re-snapshot after any page change
```

Refs (`@e1`, `@e2`, ...) are assigned fresh on every snapshot. They become **stale the moment the page changes** — after clicks that navigate, form submits, dynamic re-renders, dialog opens. Always re-snapshot before your next ref interaction.

## Quickstart

```bash
# Install once
npm i -g agent-browser && agent-browser install

# Linux hosts can install required browser libraries too
agent-browser install --with-deps

# Take a screenshot of a page
agent-browser open https://example.com
agent-browser screenshot home.png
agent-browser close

# Search, click a result, and capture it
agent-browser open https://duckduckgo.com
agent-browser snapshot -i                      # find the search box ref
agent-browser fill @e1 "agent-browser cli"
agent-browser press Enter
agent-browser wait --load networkidle
agent-browser snapshot -i                      # refs now reflect results
agent-browser click @e5                        # click a result
agent-browser screenshot result.png
```

The browser stays running across commands so these feel like a single session. Use `agent-browser close` (or `close --all`) when you're done.

## MCP integration

For tools that support Model Context Protocol servers, start the stdio server:

```bash
agent-browser mcp
agent-browser mcp --tools all
agent-browser mcp --tools core,network,react
```

Configure the MCP client to launch `agent-browser` with `["mcp"]`. The server defaults to MCP protocol 2025-11-25 and accepts older supported client protocol versions during initialization. The default tools profile is `core`, which keeps MCP context small for everyday browser automation. Use `--tools all` for the full typed CLI parity surface, or combine profiles with commas, such as `--tools core,network,react`. Profiles are `core`, `network`, `state`, `debug`, `tabs`, `react`, `mobile`, and `all`; the `debug` profile includes plugin registry and command.run tools. Each tool accepts typed arguments plus `extraArgs` for advanced CLI flags and exact CLI parity. The common `allowedDomains` array maps to `--allowed-domains` and activates the same WebRTC containment and launch-mode restrictions. Tool discovery is paginated and includes read-only/open-world annotations so modern MCP clients can load the large typed surface incrementally. Use the tool `session` argument or `AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION` to isolate browser sessions.

## eve agent integration

For eve agents, mount the `@agent-browser/eve` extension instead of hand-writing browser tools. It adds namespaced tools such as `browser__navigate`, `browser__snapshot`, `browser__click`, `browser__fill`, `browser__find`, and `browser__screenshot`, all backed by agent-browser running inside the eve sandbox. The sandbox bootstrap helpers (`installAgentBrowser`, `agentBrowserRevalidationKey`) ship with the same package under `@agent-browser/eve/sandbox`, so `agent/sandbox.ts` needs no extra dependency.

## Reading a page

```bash
agent-browser snapshot                    # full tree (verbose)
agent-browser snapshot -i                 # interactive elements only (preferred)
agent-browser snapshot -i -u              # include href urls on links
agent-browser snapshot -i -c              # compact (no empty structural nodes)
agent-browser snapshot -i -d 3            # cap depth at 3 levels
agent-browser snapshot -s "#main"         # scope to a CSS selector
agent-browser snapshot -i --json          # machine-readable output
```

Snapshot output looks like:

```
Page: Example - Log in
URL: https://example.com/login

@e1 [heading] "Log in"
@e2 [form]
  @e3 [input type="email"] placeholder="Email"
  @e4 [input type="password"] placeholder="Password"
  @e5 [button type="submit"] "Continue"
  @e6 [link] "Forgot password?"
```

For unstructured reading (no refs needed):

```bash
agent-browser read                         # read rendered active-tab DOM
agent-browser read https://docs.example.com/guide  # docs-friendly fetch, prefers markdown
agent-browser read https://docs.example.com/guide --filter auth  # one matching section
agent-browser read https://docs.example.com/guide --outline  # compact page headings
agent-browser read https://docs.example.com --llms index --filter auth  # compact llms.txt discovery
agent-browser get text @e1                # visible text of an element
agent-browser get html @e1                # innerHTML
agent-browser get attr @e1 href           # any attribute
agent-browser get value @e1               # input value
agent-browser get title                   # page title
agent-browser get url                     # current URL
agent-browser get count ".item"           # count matching elements
```

Use `read [url]` when you need to consume documentation or other text pages rather than interact with a rendered UI. Omit the URL to read the rendered DOM of the active tab in the current browser session, including browser auth state and client-side updates. Explicit URL reads send `Accept: text/markdown`, try the same URL with `.md` appended when the first response is not markdown, walk ancestor paths toward `/` to find the nearest `llms.txt` for a matching docs link, print markdown/plain text when available, and fall back to readable text extracted from HTML without launching Chrome. Add `--filter <text>` to narrow a page to matching heading sections, `--outline` for compact headings on one page, `--llms index` for a compact nearest-ancestor `llms.txt` link list, and `--llms full` only when you explicitly need `llms-full.txt`. With `--llms` or `--require-md`, omitting the URL uses the active tab URL because those modes depend on HTTP resources. With `--llms` or `--outline`, `--filter <text>` narrows links, sections, or headings. Add `--require-md` when you specifically want to verify markdown negotiation, `--raw` when you need the response body unchanged, and `--json` when you need metadata such as `source` and `contentType`. Global safeguards such as `--allowed-domains`, `--content-boundaries`, and `--max-output` also apply to read fetches and output.

For sessions that handle sensitive data, use `--allowed-domains` to restrict navigations and page-initiated network traffic. Supported Chromium sessions also disable `RTCPeerConnection` while the allowlist is active so WebRTC STUN, TURN, and related DNS traffic cannot bypass the HTTP filter. Dedicated and shared workers are guarded with a bootstrap wrapper; if a page CSP forbids that wrapper, the worker fails closed rather than running without the allowlist guard. Pre-existing CDP sessions, auto-connect, Chrome profiles, direct-page provider plugins, agent-browser restore or state-file replay, raw Chrome args that select profiles, restore sessions, or open startup pages, iOS, and Safari reject this option because agent-browser cannot install equivalent containment before page scripts run. This is browser-level containment, not an operating-system firewall; see [Trust boundaries](references/trust-boundaries.md) for deployment guidance.

## Interacting

```bash
agent-browser click @e1                   # click
agent-browser click @e1 --new-tab         # open link in new tab instead of navigating
agent-browser dblclick @e1                # double-click
agent-browser hover @e1                   # hover

**Site 1 of 5: aarronwalter.com**

What stands out:
1. **Animated line field.** Thin flowing lines drawn on canvas sit behind everything. They move without competing with the text.
2. **Huge name as the hero.** No photo. One thin accent rule, a short bio, and small uppercase social links.
3. **Work as a numbered list.** Big company names (01–05), with role and years on the right. On hover the name turns lime and the arrow turns blue.
4. **Restrained palette.** Near-black background, warm off-white text, one lime accent.
5. **Has a colophon.** You already mentioned that one.

Their trade-off: it's a Next.js site with about 10 JS bundles, all for one look.

**What do you like here?** Pick numbers or tell me in your own words. Anything you dislike is useful too.

I like the subtle background animation. Not necessarily the exact lines, but the idea of it. Just adds a little more depth to things. I love the use of the full browser width. Works very well responsively. Yes, I like the larger name, no photo, short bio with social links. I like the typography, font choices he used. You can tell he has a design background. He used Claude to build this though. He has a Colophon page discussing the site and how he designed/built it. https://aarronwalter.com/colophon 

I like the overall look and feel of the site. Not necessarily the colors, or specific fonts, or anything I want to completely copy, but just the overall aesthetics of it, I really like.

# Colophon

For the curious, and for my own memory, here's how this site came to be.

Process

## My Collaborator

I designed and built this site working with Claude Code, Anthropic’s agentic coding tool, as an experiment and a learning process. Designing a personal website is, in my experience, one of the hardest projects. The mix of blank-canvas freedom, deep personal investment, and the gap between ideas and execution tends to make them stall. Claude Code narrowed that gap in a way I hadn’t experienced before. I could stay focused on creative decisions rather than getting lost in implementation details. That’s new for me, and a little magical.

Because AI-assisted workflows are new to most of us, it feels worth describing how the collaboration actually went. As with any design project, I brought my own ideas about concept, color palette, typography, information hierarchy, and the overall user experience. I shared those with Claude Code, who in turn opened my eyes to ways I could extend them using technical solutions I wouldn’t have reached on my own. I’ve spent years teaching design, front-end, and server-side development, and I’ve built plenty of sites and apps, solo and with collaborators. This felt like old times sitting next to an engineer who helped bring my ideas to life and contributed her own. I never once felt like I was abdicating creativity. Quite the opposite. I felt more in touch with it.

I was occasionally in the code making my own tweaks, but I can’t hold a candle to what Claude can do there. I never opened a Figma file to figure out layout. I designed in the browser, which feels truer to the medium. Designing a picture of a website and then turning it into the real thing has always struck me as a silly way to do things. It tied my hands. I don’t think I’ll go back.

The Feels

## Design Influences

The visual language of the site draws from a few places. The stacked ridgeline plot in this header is not synthetic — it’s actual radio emission data from PSR B1919+21, the first radio pulsar ever discovered, recorded at 318 MHz by Harold Craft at Arecibo Observatory in 1970. Peter Saville used the same dataset for Joy Division’s Unknown Pleasures cover. The subtle animation reflects the pulsar’s actual 1.3373-second period.

The sounds of Hans Zimmer, Tangerine Dream, Boards of Canada, and Carbon Based Lifeforms were playing while I designed this site. No doubt this music influenced things.

Typography

## Typefaces

Display headings are set in F37 Lineca by F37 Foundry— a contemporary serif with an optical elegance that holds up at both large and small sizes. Its slightly negative sidebearing at display scale gives the headings their tight, confident stance.

Body copy, labels, and UI text are set in Aktiv Grotesk by Dalton Maag, served via Adobe Fonts. It pairs well with Lineca without competing.

Jedi knights vex Sith lords by quickly zapping the forgotten Wampa.F37 Lineca — Display

Joy quivers as love tears us apart; bleak fog hazes my dim, wrecked exit now.Aktiv Grotesk — Body

Audio Nerdery

## Sound Setup

Music matters to me, and dialing in the right listening experience is half the fun. After plenty of tinkering, here’s the setup that keeps me happy in the studio: a Thorens TD125 Mk II turntable, a McIntosh MA5100 integrated amp, and a pair of Klipsch Heresy IV speakers. Warm sound, beautiful objects. My kids will fight over this gear when I die.

Accessibility

## WCAG 2.1 AA

The site targets WCAG 2.1 Level AA compliance. A full audit was conducted covering landmark roles, heading structure, image alt text, keyboard navigation, focus management, color contrast, and motion preferences. All decorative canvas animations are hidden for users who have enabled prefers-reduced-motionin their OS settings. The lightbox, hamburger navigation, and contact form all have proper focus management so keyboard and screen reader users aren’t left stranded.

If you spot something that feels off, please file a bug.

Under the Hood

Yeah, this one didn't necessarily have anything specific that I really liked. It was just another example of something a little different from your typical standard personal sites you see out there. input.content:
# Design directions (Phase 1, step 2)

Three directions to prototype in code. Each has a **different page topology**, so they should look different even in grayscale (the failure of the old comp rounds).
North star: **"This is Jarod. Definitely Jarod."** Sources: [inspiration.md](inspiration.md), IDEATION.md, CONTENT.md.

The two that aren't picked become **Remix candidates**. They stay candidates until the Phase 1 smoke test proves they can share the chosen markup.

---

## A. Backstage ⭐ recommended default

**Idea:** literally "the work behind the work." A polished front layer sits on top of a visible backstage: the grid, registration marks, spacing rhythm and token annotations the page is built on.

- **Topology:** layered. Full-bleed backstage plane (blueprint-style grid, crop marks at section corners) under "front sheets" that hold content. Pillars are **stacked, numbered sheets** that pile up as you scroll (gertix). Sticky section labels.
- **Definitely Jarod because:** his tagline, three design systems founded, and his job has always been the scaffolding that makes other people fast. The site shows its own scaffolding.
- **Ambient motion is made of:** **the site's own tokens.** Grid spacing *is* the spacing scale, line weight *is* the border knob. Idle: the grid breathes very slightly. On Remix, the backstage visibly re-measures itself (density changes → grid re-spaces). Real data, and only this site can have it.
- **Interactive moment:** **"Peek backstage."** Hover or focus a section and a redline overlay shows what it's made of (spacing, type step, token names). It's the IDEATION "Redline" idea used as an easter egg, not the whole page.
- **Imagery without photos:** line-art illustrations per pillar, drawn with tokens (stroke = border knob, color = accent role), so they Remix too.
- **5-second recruiter read:** huge name on the front sheet, role line, one-sentence bio, stats row (18 years · 12+ leading · 40-person global org · 3 design systems founded), Let's talk.
- **Risk:** it's about the work more than the person. Mitigated by voice, the About section, and the writing.

## B. Edition

**Idea:** he started in 2008 as an interface designer at **The Dallas Morning News**. The site is a modern editorial broadsheet: his name as the nameplate, his career as front-page stories, and the writing has an obvious home.

- **Topology:** multi-column editorial grid. Nameplate masthead, dateline ("FRISCO, TX"), asymmetric columns, heavy rules, pull quotes for testimonials, "above the fold" literally means something.
- **Definitely Jarod because:** newsroom origin, self-taught designer, and a writer now publishing. It carries the **personal** side better than A.
- **Ambient motion is made of:** **the site being built in public.** A slow wire ticker of real activity from the repo and the writing (latest commit, newest post, current workbench status). It's quiet, typographic and true.
- **Interactive moment:** **"Edition" switcher.** Remix framed as editions (morning, evening, special), a natural metaphor for re-skinning the same stories.
- **Imagery without photos:** typographic: drop caps, big numerals, rules, ink texture.
- **5-second recruiter read:** headline = role line, lede = bio, a "by the numbers" sidebar, contact in the masthead.
- **Risk:** literary tone could overshadow the engineering, so outcomes must stay prominent.

## C. Threads

**Idea:** "an ADHD brain running twenty threads at once" and "18 years, one throughline" (both from CONTENT.md). Many fine threads, one bold throughline that ties his story together.

- **Topology:** a single narrative spine. One continuous throughline runs down the page and links sections (hero → work → pillars → career → contact). The career section is the only true timeline: the thread splits by company, with real years.
- **Definitely Jarod because:** the most personal of the three. ADHD, systems as external executive function, and the same problem chased for 18 years with bigger leverage each time.
- **Ambient motion is made of:** **his career data.** Each thread is a real role, from start year to end year (2008 → today). Threads converge where roles overlap. Not decorative noise.
- **Interactive moment:** hover a thread to light up what it connects to (a role, its outcomes, a pillar).
- **Imagery without photos:** the threads themselves, plus line-art per pillar.
- **5-second recruiter read:** name, role line and bio sit at the start of the throughline; stats sit on it as the first "stops".
- **Risks:** must not read as Aarron Walter's line field (that's why ours is interactive, data-bound and tied to sections, not a background texture). Timeline motion stays *inside* the career section, never whole-page scroll hijacking.

---

## Not chosen as defaults (possible Remix alternates later)
- **Editor theme** (Catppuccin/Dracula vibe): works best as a Remix brand, not the default. That avoids the fake-terminal gimmick on first load.
- **Zen Garden, grown up:** belongs in the **Remix** framing itself (the Remix panel can nod to it explicitly).

## How prototypes get built (decision)
- Prototypes are **throwaway HTML/CSS in `prototypes/`**, outside `src/`. Never deployed, and the CI guards stay untouched (no loosening).
- Each covers the **hero + first section** at 390px and 1440px.
- The chosen direction gets **rebuilt properly on the token pipeline** in the smoke-test step. That rebuild is the real Remix test.

content.text:
I combined the five sites with your IDEATION notes into three directions. Each has a different page structure, so they'd look different even in grayscale.

**A. Backstage** ⭐ my pick
- "The work behind the work" taken literally: a polished front layer over a visible backstage of grid lines, crop marks and token annotations.
- The background animation is drawn from the site's own tokens, so when Remix changes the spacing, the backdrop re-measures itself.
- The interactive moment: "peek backstage" on a section to see what it's built from.

**B. Edition**
- Built on your Dallas Morning News start: a modern broadsheet with your name as the masthead and your career as front-page stories.
- A quiet live ticker shows what's being built in public: latest commit, newest post.
- Remix becomes "editions": morning, evening, special.

**C. Threads**
- Built on your "twenty threads at once" and "18 years, one throughline" lines.
- One bold line connects the whole page.
- The background threads are your real roles and years.
- It's the most personal of the three.

Whichever two you don't pick become candidates for the Remix alternate brands. Each direction's full write-up (motion, imagery, what a recruiter sees in 5 seconds, risks) is in `docs/design/directions.md`.

**One question: should I build quick coded prototypes of all three?** Each would be the hero plus the first section, at phone and desktop width, so you can compare them in the browser.
I'm leaning towards the backstage one as well. Do you think we should just roll with that or knock out a few prototypes before deciding?

I'd go with Backstage, but still prototype it. Build 2–3 versions of Backstage itself rather than all three directions.

1. **The concept is settled.** We both lean A, and the other two can still come back as Remix alternate brands. Prototyping B and C now would be effort spent on directions we're probably not choosing.
2. **What's open is how it's carried out.** That's where the old image comps failed: they had ideas but missed on execution. How visible should the backstage be? Barely there, clearly present, or front and center? You'll only know by seeing it.
3. **Prototypes are cheap.** An agent builds them quickly, and you compare them in a real browser at phone and desktop width.

**The plan:**
- **3 Backstage versions**, each covering the hero plus the first section:
  - **Whisper:** the grid and crop marks are barely visible, and the peek-backstage effect does most of the work.
  - **Blueprint:** the backstage is clearly present, with the stacked sheets and annotations always visible.
  - **Exposed:** a loud, structural, editorial take with the scaffolding as part of the look.
- Same copy and same content in all three. Only the treatment changes.
- You pick one, or mix parts ("Blueprint's hero with Whisper's restraint").

Should I set Backstage as the direction and build these three?
Yep, let's rock n' roll!
